challenges.name: resources-variables-outputs-quiz
challenges.title: Read the first plans
challenges.description: Three statements about what Rice Rocket saw the first time it ran `terraform plan` on infrastructure that used to be clicked together in the AWS console. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Ask who decides an `arn` or an `id`: you in the configuration, or the cloud provider when the object is created?
Run the plan in your head with `-input=false`, as CI does: where could a value for a variable with no default come from?
Terraform's state maps each resource address (`aws_s3_bucket.uploads`) to one real object. What does a new address look like to it?

questions.question:
The first plan for the uploads bucket shows:

```text
  # aws_s3_bucket.uploads will be created
  + resource "aws_s3_bucket" "uploads" {
      + arn                         = (known after apply)
      + bucket                      = "rice-rocket-staging-uploads"
      + bucket_domain_name          = (known after apply)
      + id                          = (known after apply)
      + tags                        = {
          + "Environment" = "staging"
          + "Project"     = "rice-rocket"
        }
    }

Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
```

Statement: "`arn` and `id` are set by AWS when the bucket is created, so the plan cannot know them yet; any value built from them is also `(known after apply)`."
questions.explanation: True. Attributes you set (`bucket`, `tags`) are known at plan time. Computed attributes are filled in by the provider from the API's answer after the object exists, so the plan shows `(known after apply)`. An expression that uses them, like `aws_s3_bucket.uploads.arn` in an output or another resource, is unknown in the same plan. The misconception is that a plan has asked AWS for those values.

questions.question:
The CI job runs the plan without a value for `env`:

```hcl
variable "env" {
  type = string
}
```

```text
$ terraform plan -input=false
```

Statement: "Terraform treats a variable with no default and no value as an empty string, so the plan names the bucket `rice-rocket--uploads` and carries on."
questions.explanation: False. A variable without a default is required. Interactively Terraform asks for it; with `-input=false` (as in CI) the plan stops with an error saying no value was given for the required variable `env`. Values come from `-var`, `-var-file`, `*.auto.tfvars` files or `TF_VAR_env`. The misconception is that missing variables default to empty, which would silently create wrongly named resources.

questions.question:
A teammate renamed the resource label to read better and planned again:

```diff
- resource "aws_s3_bucket" "uploads" {
+ resource "aws_s3_bucket" "user_uploads" {
    bucket = "rice-rocket-staging-uploads"
  }
```

```text
  # aws_s3_bucket.uploads will be destroyed
  # aws_s3_bucket.user_uploads will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
```

Statement: "State maps each resource address to one real object, so a renamed label looks like a new resource and the old one gets destroyed, unless a `moved` block says the two addresses are the same object."
questions.explanation: True. Terraform does not compare bucket names to guess that two resources are the same: state stores `aws_s3_bucket.uploads` -> the real bucket, and `aws_s3_bucket.user_uploads` has no entry, so it plans a create and a destroy (which would fail anyway on a bucket that still holds objects, or worse succeed on an empty one). A `moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.uploads  to = aws_s3_bucket.user_uploads }` block turns the change into a rename in state; lesson 5 covers it. Resource labels are part of the identity, not cosmetics.

challenges.name: uploads-bucket-and-logs
challenges.title: Describe the uploads bucket and the api logs
challenges.description: Until now Rice Rocket's uploads bucket and the api's log group were clicked together in the AWS console, once per environment, with small differences nobody could explain. The editor holds `infra/main.tf` with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `# [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that: `env` accepts only `staging` or `production` (error message `env must be staging or production.`); every name starts with `rice-rocket-<env>` and every resource that takes tags gets `Project`, `Environment` and `ManagedBy`; the bucket `rice-rocket-<env>-uploads` keeps old versions and blocks public access; the versioning and public access settings follow whichever bucket the environment creates; the api log group `/rice-rocket-<env>/api` keeps logs 30 days in production and 7 elsewhere; and the outputs give the bucket's name and ARN. Run plans the file for staging and production with a plan simulator.
hints: Plan it for two environments in your head: which values must change with `env`, and which resources must point at the bucket instead of at its name written out?

Look at a `validation` block inside `variable`, a `locals` block, string templates `"${local.name}-uploads"`, references like `aws_s3_bucket.uploads.id`, a conditional `a ? b : c`, and `output` blocks.

A queue per environment with a dead-letter queue looks like: `locals { name = "shop-${var.stage}" }`, `resource "aws_sqs_queue" "dlq" { name = "${local.name}-dlq" }`, `resource "aws_sqs_queue" "jobs" { name = "${local.name}-jobs"  message_retention_seconds = var.stage == "prod" ? 1209600 : 345600  redrive_policy = jsonencode({ deadLetterTargetArn = aws_sqs_queue.dlq.arn, maxReceiveCount = 5 }) }`, and `output "jobs_url" { value = aws_sqs_queue.jobs.url }`.
